---
title: "Part 1 - Intro to coding with R"
---

# Welcome! In this part we will learn just enough R to read the code in the rest of the session. Click the green "play" arrow at the top right of each gray code chunk to run it; the results appear right below the chunk.

# First, we load the packages we will use. A package is a set of machines (functions) somebody else built, so we don't have to.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(immunogenetr)
```

# R as a calculator. Run this chunk and you are officially an R coder!

```{r}
2 + 2
```

# Objects: we store something in an object (a labeled bin) with the arrow "\<-", then use the name of the bin instead of the thing itself.

```{r}
typing <- c("HLA-A*02:01:01:01", "HLA-A*68:01:02:01", "HLA-B*07:02:01:01")

typing
```

# Functions: a machine that takes something in, does something to it, and gives something back. HLA_truncate() is a function from immunogenetr. Arguments (like "fields") are its settings.

```{r}
HLA_truncate(typing)
```

# You can always learn about how a function works by using "?" to open its help page.

```{r}
?HLA_truncate
```

# The pipe "\|\>" is the conveyor belt: it feeds what's on its left into the function on its right. Read it as "then".

```{r}
typing |>
  HLA_truncate() |>
  first()
```

# Most lab data lives in tables (data frames). immunogenetr comes with a few examples; HLA_dictionary is a small sample of the 2008 HLA dictionary.

```{r}
HLA_dictionary
```

# We can perform several steps in sequence by stringing functions together. The tidyverse verbs filter() (pick rows), mutate() (make columns) and select() (pick columns) are chained together below:

```{r}
HLA_dictionary |>
  filter(WHO.Assigned.Type == "A11") |>
  mutate(two_field = HLA_truncate(HLA.Allele)) |>
  select(two_field, WHO.Assigned.Type) 
```

# That's all the R we need: packages, objects, functions, the pipe, and tables. Everything else is just more functions, and the rest of today is about the functions people have already built for HLA labs.
